concepts.title: Structure of a Neuron and Nerve Impulse Transmission
concepts.definition: The nervous' primary cellular unit system specialized for receiving, processing, and transmitting information through electrical and chemical signals.
concepts.formula: concept method; no single closed formula
concepts.key_idea: Nerve impulses travel electrically within a neuron and chemically across the synaptic gap between neurons.
question_patterns: explain how information travels through a neuron
what happens at the synapse between two neurons
describe the structure of a nerve cell
where is information acquired and converted into electrical signals in a neuron
justify why structure of a neuron and nerve impulse transmission matters

solution_steps.action: Identify the site of signal acquisition
solution_steps.explain: The dendritic tips of the neuron detect environmental stimuli or receive chemical signals from preceding cells.
The signal triggers a chemical reaction generating an electrical impulse that travels through the cell body and along the axon.
At the axon terminal, the electrical impulse triggers the release of neurotransmitter chemicals that diffuse across the synapse to initiate an impulse in the next neuron.

concepts.title: Reflex Action and Reflex Arc
concepts.definition: An immediate, involuntary response to an environmental stimulus that is processed directly through a short neural pathway in the spinal cord to minimize harm.
concepts.formula: concept method; no single closed formula
concepts.key_idea: Reflex arcs bypass conscious brain thought to execute rapid, protective motor actions.
question_patterns: what is a reflex action
explain the pathway of a reflex arc
how does the body respond to a hot object reflexively
what is the role of the spinal cord in reflex actions
describe reflex action and reflex arc with an example

solution_steps.explain: A receptor (e.g., heat receptor in skin) detects an environmental change.
The sensory neuron carries the electrical impulse from the receptor to the spinal cord.
In the spinal cord, an association/relay neuron integrates the input and transfers it directly to a motor neuron.

solution_steps.action: Execute response via motor neuron and effector
solution_steps.explain: The motor neuron transmits the impulse to the effector muscle, causing it to contract and move away from the stimulus.

concepts.title: Regions and Functions of the Human Brain
concepts.definition: The nervous' central organ system that integrates sensory inputs and coordinates both voluntary and involuntary bodily activities.
concepts.formula: concept method; no single closed formula
concepts.key_idea: The brain is divided into fore-brain, mid-brain, and hind-brain, each managing distinct cognitive and physiological functions.
question_patterns: what are the main regions of the human brain
which part of the brain maintains posture and balance
explain the functions of the fore-brain, mid-brain, and hind-brain
how do we feel full or detect hunger in the brain
give one everyday example of regions and functions of the human brain

solution_steps.explain: The fore-brain is the main thinking center, responsible for memory, learning, sensory interpretation, and hunger sensation.

solution_steps.action: Identify mid-brain and hind-brain involuntary controls
solution_steps.explain: The mid-brain and medulla (hind-brain) control involuntary actions like blood pressure, salivation, and vomiting.
The cerebellum (part of hind-brain) coordinates voluntary movements, precision, and maintains body posture and equilibrium.

concepts.title: Protection of the Central Nervous System
concepts.definition: The structural defenses, including the bony cranium, vertebral column, and cerebrospinal fluid, that shield the both brain and spinal cord from mechanical injuries.
concepts.formula: concept method; no single closed formula
concepts.key_idea: Bony enclosures and shock-absorbing fluid protect the delicate tissues of the central nervous system.
question_patterns: how is the brain protected from shocks
what protects the spinal cord in human beings
explain the role of the vertebral column and bony box
justify why protection of the central nervous system matters
explain protection of the central nervous system in your own words

solution_steps.explain: The brain is housed inside a bony skull (cranium) and suspended in a fluid-filled balloon (cerebrospinal fluid) that acts as a shock absorber.
The spinal cord is protected by the vertebral column (backbone), which is a hard, bony structure running down the back.

solution_steps.action: Explain the role of cerebrospinal fluid
solution_steps.explain: Cerebrospinal fluid surrounds both the brain and spinal cord, cushioning them against mechanical shocks and maintaining a stable chemical environment.

concepts.title: Cellular Mechanism of Muscle Contraction
concepts.definition: The process where muscle cells alter their both shape and shorten through the rearrangement of specialized proteins triggered by nervous stimulation.
concepts.formula: concept method; no single closed formula
concepts.key_idea: Electrical nerve impulses stimulate cellular protein changes that cause muscle fibers to contract.
question_patterns: how does muscle tissue cause movement
what happens to muscle cells when a nerve impulse reaches them
explain how muscle cells change their shape
how does cellular mechanism of muscle contraction work
list the main features of cellular mechanism of muscle contraction

solution_steps.explain: The nervous impulse reaches the neuromuscular junction, stimulating the muscle fiber.
Specialized proteins in the muscle cells change their shape and organization in response to the electrical signal.
The new protein arrangements cause the muscle cells to contract and shorten, resulting in movement.

concepts.title: Immediate Growth-Independent Movements in Plants
concepts.definition: Rapid, non-directional plant movements triggered by touch or other stimuli, achieved through reversible changes in cellular water content rather than growth.
concepts.formula: concept method; no single closed formula
concepts.key_idea: Turgor pressure changes in plant cells enable fast, growth-independent responses like leaf folding.
question_patterns: how do the leaves of a sensitive plant fold up
explain immediate response to stimulus in mimosa pudica
how is plant movement independent of growth achieved
compare animal muscle movement with sensitive plant leaf movement
how does immediate growth-independent movements in plants work

solution_steps.explain: Touch is detected, and electrochemical signals are transmitted from cell to cell without specialized nervous tissue.
Target cells change their shape by losing or gaining water, causing them to shrink or swell.
The sudden loss of turgor pressure in specific cells causes the leaves to fold up and droop.

concepts.title: Directional Growth Movements (Tropisms)
concepts.definition: Slow, directional growth responses of plant organs toward or away from environmental stimuli such as light, gravity, water, or chemicals.
concepts.formula: concept method; no single closed formula
concepts.key_idea: Tropic movements orient plant parts favorably in response to external directional cues.
question_patterns: what is phototropism and geotropism
explain chemotropism with an example
how do plant roots and shoots respond to gravity
describe how tendrils circle around a support
short note on directional growth movements (tropisms)

solution_steps.explain: Environmental triggers like light (phototropism), gravity (geotropism), water (hydrotropism), or chemicals (chemotropism) act as directional cues.
Cells on one side of the plant organ grow faster than those on the other side, causing the organ to bend.
Shoots bend toward light (positive phototropism) and away from gravity, while roots grow toward gravity (positive geotropism) and water.

concepts.title: Functions of Phytohormones
concepts.definition: Naturally occurring organic compounds in plants that regulate growth, cell division, development, and physiological responses to environmental stimuli.
concepts.formula: concept method; no single closed formula
concepts.key_idea: Plant hormones like auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, and abscisic acid coordinate growth and inhibition.
question_patterns: what are plant hormones
how does auxin help a plant bend towards light
name a plant hormone that inhibits growth
what are the roles of gibberellins and cytokinins
what do you understand by functions of phytohormones

solution_steps.explain: Auxin is synthesized at the shoot tip and diffuses to the shady side, stimulating cells there to grow longer and cause bending toward light.
Gibberellins assist in stem elongation, while cytokinins promote rapid cell division in fruits and seeds.

solution_steps.action: Explain growth inhibition by abscisic acid
solution_steps.explain: Abscisic acid signals the plant to stop growing, leading to effects like the wilting of leaves.

concepts.title: Endocrine Glands and Animal Hormones
concepts.definition: Chemical messengers secreted by ductless endocrine glands directly into the blood to regulate metabolism, growth, and physiological homeostasis across target organs.
concepts.formula: concept method; no single closed formula
concepts.key_idea: Hormones provide slow, widespread, and persistent chemical coordination throughout the animal body.
question_patterns: how does chemical coordination take place in animals
what is the role of adrenaline in emergency situations
why is iodised salt advisable for the thyroid gland
explain the functions of insulin and growth hormone
justify why endocrine glands and animal hormones matters

solution_steps.explain: Secreted by adrenal glands, adrenaline increases heart rate and breathing, diverting blood to skeletal muscles to prepare for fight-or-flight.
The thyroid gland requires iodine to synthesize thyroxin, which regulates carbohydrate, protein, and fat metabolism for balanced growth.
Growth hormone from the pituitary regulates development, while insulin from the pancreas regulates blood glucose levels.

concepts.title: Feedback Control of Hormone Secretion
concepts.definition: A self-regulating biological mechanism that adjusts the timing and quantity of hormone release using the concentration of specific substances in the blood.
concepts.formula: concept method; no single closed formula
concepts.key_idea: Feedback loops ensure hormones are indeed secreted in precise amounts to maintain internal balance.
question_patterns: how is the timing and amount of hormone release regulated
explain the feedback mechanism of insulin secretion
what happens when blood sugar levels rise
give one everyday example of feedback control of hormone secretion
short note on feedback control of hormone secretion

solution_steps.explain: High blood glucose levels are detected by the cells of the pancreas.
The pancreas responds by secreting more insulin to lower blood glucose levels.
As blood sugar levels fall, the stimulus is removed, and insulin secretion is reduced.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A plant shoot bends towards a light source placed on its {direction} side. Explain the role of the hormone {hormone_name} in this movement.

extracted_variables.direction: the side from which light is coming

solution_template.explain: The hormone {hormone_name} (auxin) is synthesized at the growing tip of the plant shoot.

solution_template.action: Explain diffusion to the shady side
solution_template.explain: When light comes from the {direction} side, the hormone diffuses towards the opposite, shady side of the shoot.
The high concentration of {hormone_name} on the shady side stimulates cells to grow longer, causing the shoot to bend towards the light.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A person is in a highly stressful or scary situation. Explain how the hormone {hormone_name} secreted by the {gland_name} gland prepares the body to deal with this emergency.

extracted_variables.gland_name: the endocrine gland secreting the hormone

solution_template.explain: The hormone {hormone_name} (adrenaline) is secreted directly into the blood by the {gland_name} (adrenal) glands.

solution_template.action: Describe physiological changes in target organs
solution_template.explain: It acts on the heart, causing it to beat faster to supply more oxygen to muscles, while reducing blood flow to the skin and digestive system.
Breathing rate increases due to contractions of diaphragm and rib muscles, preparing the body to run or fight.
